method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

sourceChecks.supports: Initial back placement; firm flat clear sleep space; no need to repeatedly reposition an independently rolling infant. Targeted retrieval supports101–106 and revised106 direction.
Immediate medical attention for suspected swallowing of one or more magnets; supports109 key.
Keep cords inaccessible, avoid cribs/furniture near reachable cords, and replace accessible corded coverings; supports120.

items.assessment: Choking fear provides a relevant misconception; consistent supine placement is correct for a healthy infant and positional alternatives are plausible parental practices.
Leaving a sleeping child in a car seat after travel is a relevant applied hazard. Flat suitable sleep surface is clearly best; alternatives are plausible attempted positional fixes.
The parent proposes crib padding; the answer and distractors test actual risk misconceptions about thin bumpers, toy location, and remote monitoring.
The separate sleep surface key is sound; adding pillows and moving to a sofa are very easy foils.
issues: The separate sleep surface key is sound; adding pillows and moving to a sofa are very easy foils.
proposedChanges: Use a fatigued breastfeeding parent and compare returning infant to bedside bassinet, asking an awake adult to monitor while bed-sharing, using a recliner for feeds, and placing infant on the adult mattress away from pillows. Keep clear safest-plan wording and explain risks respectfully.

items.assessment: Product marketing cues versus actual suitability are relevant to parent education. Breathable fabric, supervision, and short naps are credible misconceptions; key is defensible.
This generic SATA repeats101/103 almost entirely and has no patient-specific evaluation evidence despite application label.
issues: This generic SATA repeats101/103 almost entirely and has no patient-specific evaluation evidence despite application label.
proposedChanges: Use an older infant newly rolling independently and caregiver statements: continuing initial supine placement, avoiding wedges, whether repositioning every time is required, and maintaining a clear sleep space. Verify current Health Canada rolling guidance. This provides a distinct decision instead of repeating the same crib list.

items.assessment: Asymptomatic suspected button-battery ingestion is time-critical. Observation/stool monitoring/feeding are recognizable home-management mistakes, with clear rationales.
Secure storage is correct but tissue wrapping is a weak protective alternative.
issues: Secure storage is correct but tissue wrapping is a weak protective alternative.
proposedChanges: Compare a locked high cupboard, original packaging in the low drawer, separating used from new batteries, and a lidded container on a reachable shelf. Keep focus on access despite packaging or battery charge state.

items.assessment: Immediate medical evaluation for suspected multiple magnets is correct and primary guidance confirms it. Routine-visit radiograph is an implausible delay choice.
issues: Immediate medical evaluation for suspected multiple magnets is correct and primary guidance confirms it. Routine-visit radiograph is an implausible delay choice.
proposedChanges: Replace that option with arranging a next-day primary-care assessment or monitoring until the next stool. Add direct Health Canada magnet-safety source, since existing a-child notes full page not verified.

items.assessment: Separating small parts is correct; bright colour and one-piece-at-a-time are filler.
issues: Separating small parts is correct; bright colour and one-piece-at-a-time are filler.
proposedChanges: Use shared play space with older sibling and compare a separate play/storage area, supervising shared construction play, teaching the toddler not to mouth pieces, and inspecting the set for damaged pieces. Explain developmental mouthing and access control.

items.assessment: Removing balloon fragments is correct; washing fragments and watching from another room are implausible.
issues: Removing balloon fragments is correct; washing fragments and watching from another room are implausible.
proposedChanges: Compare removing fragments, allowing use of larger balloon pieces, replacing broken fragments with uninflated balloons, and supervising balloon play at the table. Explain that flexible balloon material itself is a choking hazard.

items.assessment: Original secure containers, separate storage, and child-resistant limits are correct; decanting into drink bottles is a common concrete poisoning hazard rather than an unrelated foil.
Immediate access control is correct but annual medication review, asking toddler to close bag, and checking prescription status are implausible priorities.
issues: Immediate access control is correct but annual medication review, asking toddler to close bag, and checking prescription status are implausible priorities.
proposedChanges: Compare securing the bag, checking caps are child-resistant, asking visitor to supervise the bag, and moving pill bottles into a nearby drawer. Explain why reliable restricted access is needed.

items.assessment: Stable awake child and unidentified chemical support prompt poison-service advice. Induced emesis, neutralizing remedies, and symptom waiting are real management misconceptions; rationale is sound.
Child-resistant does not mean child-proof, but liquid-only protection and label removal are cartoon distractors.
issues: Child-resistant does not mean child-proof, but liquid-only protection and label removal are cartoon distractors.
proposedChanges: Use actual caregiver statements such as storing locked and out of reach, relying on the cap after each dose, transferring daily doses to a bedside organizer, and placing bottles on a high open shelf. Either label foundation or frame teach-back evaluation.

items.assessment: Answering the door creates a practical supervision decision. Young sibling, bath seat, and open-door alternatives reflect common misconceptions; capable continuous supervision is correct.
Supervision plus appropriate flotation is correct; two pairs of arm bands and increasing distance are too obvious.
issues: Supervision plus appropriate flotation is correct; two pairs of arm bands and increasing distance are too obvious.
proposedChanges: Compare an attentive adult within reach using fitted approved equipment, moving nearer while keeping arm bands, relying on the pool lifeguard, and scheduling swimming lessons. Use similar-length options, avoiding a uniquely comprehensive key.

items.assessment: Principles are correct but entirely and toys replacing supervision advertise both nonkeys; substantial overlap with117.
issues: Principles are correct but entirely and toys replacing supervision advertise both nonkeys; substantial overlap with117.
proposedChanges: Use a handover between adults at a busy pool: explicit transfer of supervision, phone use while supervising, a properly fitted lifejacket, and assumed lifeguard coverage. Remove advertised qualifiers; explain responsibility and attention requirements.

items.assessment: Environmental fall prevention is sound; slightly wider than usual is nonsensical and curtains are weak.
issues: Environmental fall prevention is sound; slightly wider than usual is nonsensical and curtains are weak.
proposedChanges: Compare moving climbable furniture and approved opening restrictions, replacing a damaged insect screen, limiting time in the room, and teaching the child not to climb. Avoid exact opening dimensions unless sourced.

items.assessment: Accessible cord removal is sound. Decorative bow and crib-rail wrapping are implausible.
issues: Accessible cord removal is sound. Decorative bow and crib-rail wrapping are implausible.
proposedChanges: Compare moving crib and securing/replacing accessible cords, shortening the dangling cord, tying cord ends together, and installing a baby monitor. Use current Health Canada window-covering source; distinguish genuinely inaccessible cord management from a remaining reachable loop.

items.assessment: Anchoring and removing incentives are correct but allowing climbing with shoes is filler.
issues: Anchoring and removing incentives are correct but allowing climbing with shoes is filler.
proposedChanges: Compare manufacturer-directed anchoring, placing heavier items in lower drawers, moving preferred toys down, and supervising the child during play. Explain why changing incentives/weight does not replace securing tip-prone furniture; keep key concise.

items.assessment: All keys are correct, but generic visible hazards versus a locked cabinet is foundational recognition and repeats nearby items.
issues: All keys are correct, but generic visible hazards versus a locked cabinet is foundational recognition and repeats nearby items.
proposedChanges: Either honestly label foundation or add specific evidence to test whether a nominally protective measure actually prevents access (cabinet latch installed but child can release it; battery compartment requires a screw; cord inaccessible). Vary correct positions/count.

items.assessment: Concurrent alarm and headaches make evacuation urgent; ventilation, appliance investigation and battery troubleshooting are plausible but dangerous delays. Key/rationale match.
An attached garage despite an open door is a common CO misconception; outdoor placement away from openings is appropriate, with realistic ineffective ventilation alternatives.
CO-specific detection is correct but any strong gas smell and open-window substitution make the answer too easy.
issues: CO-specific detection is correct but any strong gas smell and open-window substitution make the answer too easy.
proposedChanges: Compare installing a certified CO alarm, repositioning the existing smoke alarm, arranging more frequent furnace servicing, and leaving a window partly open. Label foundation unless a specific home-assessment decision makes it applied.
